Alex Honnold Reacts to Villain Role in HBO’s Dark Wizard
World-renowned climber Alex Honnold is addressing his portrayal as a “villain” in the HBO docuseries The Dark Wizard. The series, focusing on the legacy of the late Dean Potter, examines the competitive friction between the two Yosemite icons, highlighting the psychological toll of narrative framing in high-stakes athletic legacies.
This represents more than a disagreement over a documentary’s edit; It’s a study in how media transforms raw athletic competition into a scripted morality play. When a production chooses a protagonist and an antagonist, the “villain” often finds their public legacy rewritten by editors in a room thousands of miles away from the granite walls of Yosemite National Park.
The tension arises from a fundamental clash between objective achievement and narrative necessity. In the world of elite climbing, the “first ascent” or the “first free solo” is the ultimate currency. However, in the world of prestige television, a list of achievements is boring. What sells is rivalry. What resonates is conflict. By casting Honnold as the antagonist to Potter’s visionary spirit, the series creates a dramatic arc that may prioritize entertainment over the nuanced reality of their professional relationship.
It is a precarious position to be in.
For a public figure, being the “villain” in a high-production series can have tangible effects on brand partnerships, public perception, and mental well-being. This shift in framing often necessitates a strategic response to reclaim the narrative. Many athletes in similar positions are now turning to crisis management firms to ensure their public image isn’t permanently tethered to a producer’s vision of conflict.
“The danger of the ‘villain arc’ in modern documentaries is that it replaces the complex truth of human rivalry with a binary of good versus subpar. When one subject is no longer here to provide a counter-perspective, the narrative becomes an absolute truth for the audience, regardless of its accuracy.”
The “Information Gap” in this story lies in the ethics of posthumous storytelling. As Dean Potter is no longer alive to defend his perspective or clarify his feelings, the documentary possesses an inherent power imbalance. The filmmakers hold the keys to the archive, and the surviving subject is left to react to a version of history that has already been baked into the final cut. This creates a legal and ethical minefield regarding “right of publicity” and the depiction of deceased individuals.
This is where the intersection of art and law becomes messy. Athletes and estates frequently find themselves in disputes over how their lives are curated for the screen. Navigating these portrayals often requires the intervention of entertainment lawyers who specialize in defamation and media contracts to shield individuals from damaging, though perhaps “artistically justified,” depictions.
The rivalry between Honnold and Potter reflects a broader evolution in the sport of climbing. For decades, the culture of Yosemite’s Camp 4 was defined by a certain bohemian rebellion—a rejection of mainstream success. As climbing transitioned from a fringe activity to a global spectacle, the tension between the “pure” explorer and the “competitive” athlete intensified. Honnold, with his clinical approach to risk and unprecedented visibility, represents the modern era of the sport, while Potter represented its wilder, more spiritual roots.
When these two philosophies collide on screen, the result is rarely a balanced portrait. It is a clash of archetypes.
The psychological weight of this public labeling cannot be understated. Being cast as the “bad guy” in a story about a beloved figure can lead to significant social isolation or a sense of betrayal. For high-performers who already operate in high-stress environments, the addition of public scrutiny often leads them to seek the guidance of licensed sports psychologists to manage the intersection of their private identity and their public persona.
As we see more “prestige” sports documentaries on platforms like HBO and Netflix, the trend of the “calculated rivalry” is only increasing. Producers are moving away from the traditional hagiography—the glowing portrait of a hero—and moving toward “complex” narratives that require a foil. In these stories, someone must be the obstacle. Someone must be the rival. Someone must be the villain.
The reality is that most athletic rivalries are built on mutual respect, even when that respect is buried under layers of competition and ego. The tragedy of the narrative edit is that it strips away the nuance, leaving only the conflict.
Whether the public accepts Honnold’s perspective or clings to the documentary’s framing will likely depend on which story is more compelling, not which one is more true. As the line between documentary and drama continues to blur, the ability to control one’s own story becomes the most valuable asset an athlete can possess.
